title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Control Panel
shortTitle: System Binary Proxy Execution: Control Panel
summary: Control Panel items are the settings applets users open through control.exe, and they exist as registered executable files or as .cpl files, which are dynamic-link libraries renamed and required to export a CPlApplet function. An adversary abuses this hosting model in two ways. First, a malicious Control Panel item is delivered by phishing or as a stage of multi-stage malware and run from the command line, through an application programming interface call, or by a double-click, which frequently slips past application and file extension allowlists because the extension is not treated as executable. Second, a renamed library file can be registered under a per-user Control Panel registry key, and Windows then loads it through its DllEntryPoint when the Control Panel runs, even if the file does not follow the CPL specification or export CPlApplet, so the payload executes without being directly runnable. Defensive evidence therefore spans process creation for control.exe or rundll32.exe referencing a .cpl or library file outside the system directory, writes to that per-user registration key, and image loads in control.exe or rundll32.exe from temporary and public folders. Normal Control Panel behaviour loads signed, registered applets from trusted locations and does not touch user-writable registration paths.

beginner.definition: Control Panel items are the small tools you open to change Windows settings. They are stored in files ending with .cpl, and control.exe is the program that starts them. A .cpl file is really a library file, renamed, that offers a special function.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers can build their own Control Panel item and send it by email. Many allowlists check for .exe files but forget the .cpl ending, so the file runs anyway. A library file can also be registered so Windows loads it automatically. If you ignore this, code can run from a file you never thought was executable.
howItWorks: Control Panel items are the settings tools you open, and they are stored in files ending with .cpl.
A .cpl file is a library file that has been renamed, and it must offer a function named CPlApplet.
Windows starts these tools through control.exe, or through rundll32.exe using a Control Panel function.
An attacker can build a .cpl file that runs code as soon as it is opened, then send it by email.
Another route registers a renamed library file under a per-user Control Panel registry key.
Windows then loads that file at Control Panel start and calls its entry point, even if it is not a real .cpl file.
beginner.example: In a large hotel, all staff wear a uniform, and guests trust anyone wearing one. A thief finds a spare uniform in the laundry room and walks behind the front desk. Nothing is broken and no door is forced, because the uniform is the right one. Later, the key register shows that a real key was used. A file with the .cpl ending is that uniform.
takeaways: A .cpl file is a library file with a different ending, so allowlists can miss it.
A per-user registry entry can make Windows load a renamed library file at Control Panel start.
Watch control.exe and rundll32.exe when they load files from user folders.

objectives: Explain what a Control Panel item is and how the .cpl extension relates to library files.
Describe two distinct ways an adversary abuses Control Panel hosting to gain execution.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the System Binary Proxy Execution parent technique.
Identify the registry and process telemetry that reveals malicious Control Panel items.
Explain why file extension allowlists may fail to stop this technique.
